what_its_for: Ibuprofen is used to relieve mild to moderate pain such as headaches, toothaches, muscle aches, menstrual cramps, and back pain. It also reduces fever and helps with pain and swelling caused by arthritis or minor injuries.
how_to_take: Take ibuprofen by mouth with a full glass of water (8 ounces). It is best to take it with food, milk, or an antacid to help prevent stomach upset. Do not lie down for at least 10 minutes after taking it. Swallow tablets or capsules whole — do not crush or chew them unless your product specifically says it is okay.
dosing: For adults and children 12 years and older: the usual dose is 200 to 400 mg every 4 to 6 hours as needed. Do not take more than 1,200 mg in 24 hours unless directed by your doctor. Your doctor may prescribe higher doses for certain conditions — always follow their instructions. For children under 12, ask your child's doctor or pharmacist for the right dose based on your child's weight.
missed_dose: If you are taking ibuprofen on a regular schedule and miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. However, if it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Do not double up or take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store ibuprofen at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, direct sunlight, and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep all medications out of reach of children and pets. Do not use it past the expiration date printed on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol while taking ibuprofen, as it increases your risk of stomach bleeding. Do not take other pain relievers or fever reducers (such as aspirin, naproxen, or other NSAIDs) at the same time unless your doctor says it is safe. Avoid taking ibuprofen if you have been told to avoid NSAIDs. Talk to your doctor before taking ibuprofen if you take blood thinners, steroids, or certain antidepressants. Limit caffeine, as it may worsen side effects like stomach upset.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: stomach pain, black or tarry stools, or vomiting blood (signs of stomach bleeding); chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or slurred speech (signs of heart attack or stroke); swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing (signs of a serious allergic reaction); skin rash, blisters, or peeling skin; sudden decrease in urination or swelling in your legs or feet (signs of kidney problems); yellowing of the skin or eyes (sign of liver problems). Also call your doctor if your pain or fever does not improve after 3 days, or if your symptoms get worse.
when_it_works: Ibuprofen usually starts working within 20 to 30 minutes after you take it. You should feel the full pain-relieving or fever-reducing effect within 1 to 2 hours. For conditions like arthritis, it may take several days of regular use before you notice the most benefit.
special_populations: Pregnancy: Do not use ibuprofen at 20 weeks of pregnancy or later unless specifically told to by your doctor, as it can harm the unborn baby. Avoid it especially during the last 3 months (third trimester). Breastfeeding: Small amounts pass into breast milk. Talk to your doctor before using it while breastfeeding. Elderly (65 and older): Older adults are at higher risk for stomach bleeding, kidney problems, and heart-related side effects. Use the lowest effective dose and talk to your doctor regularly. Children: Do not give ibuprofen to children under 6 months old. Always use the correct dose based on your child's weight, and use a proper measuring device for liquid forms. Kidney or liver disease: Talk to your doctor before using ibuprofen if you have kidney or liver problems, as ibuprofen may make these conditions worse. Heart disease: If you have had a heart attack, stroke, or heart surgery, talk to your doctor before using ibuprofen.
